Tip: Republic = no king.

questions.text: The principle of separation of powers aims primarily at
options: preventing tyranny and abuse of power
questions.explanation:
Concept: Separation of powers divides government into legislative, executive and judicial arms so that no single person or group can abuse power.
Step 1: Recall the purpose of separation of powers.
Step 2: It is to prevent tyranny.
Step 3: Reject executive dominance, merging the organs and eliminating the judiciary.
Answer: preventing tyranny and abuse of power.
Common mistake: Merging all powers produces tyranny, which is what the doctrine tries to avoid.
Similar example: Montesquieu said that when legislative and executive powers are united, liberty is lost.
Tip: Separate to prevent tyranny.

questions.text: The fusion of executive and legislative functions is a feature of
questions.explanation:
Concept: In the fusion of powers, the same persons belong to more than one arm of government. In a parliamentary system, ministers are also members of the legislature.
Step 1: Recall the system in which ministers sit in the legislature.
Step 2: It is the parliamentary system.
Step 3: Reject the strict presidential, confederal and federal judiciary options.
Answer: the parliamentary system.
Common mistake: Presidential systems separate executive and legislative personnel.
Similar example: The British Prime Minister is a Member of Parliament.
Tip: Parliamentary = fusion.

questions.text: The head of state in the United Kingdom is the
options: Speaker of the House of Commons
questions.explanation:
Concept: The United Kingdom's head of state is the monarch, and its head of government is the Prime Minister.
Step 1: Distinguish head of state from head of government.
Step 2: The monarch is the head of state.
Step 3: Reject the Prime Minister (head of government), the Speaker and the Chief Justice.
Answer: monarch.
Common mistake: The Prime Minister is head of government, not head of state.
Similar example: King Charles III became monarch in 2022.
Tip: UK: monarch = state, PM = government.

questions.text: Under the 1999 Constitution, the President of Nigeria is elected for a term of
questions.explanation:
Concept: Under the 1999 Constitution, the President and governors serve four-year terms, renewable once, so the maximum is eight years.
Step 1: Recall the length of the presidential term.
Step 2: It is four years, renewable once.
Step 3: Reject five years, six years non-renewable and two years.
Answer: four years, renewable once.
Common mistake: A six-year single term has been proposed by some groups but is not law.
Similar example: A governor can serve two four-year terms.
Tip: 4 + 4 = 8 years.

questions.text: In Nigeria, ministers are appointed by the
options: President, subject to confirmation by the Senate
Speaker of the House of Representatives
questions.explanation:
Concept: The President appoints ministers, but the Senate must confirm them through screening.
Step 1: Recall who appoints ministers.
Step 2: The President nominates and the Senate confirms.
Step 3: Reject the Chief Justice, the Speaker and the INEC chairman.
Answer: President, subject to confirmation by the Senate.
Common mistake: The Speaker heads the House of Representatives and does not appoint ministers.
Similar example: This is an example of a check on the executive.
Tip: President nominates, Senate confirms.

questions.text: Judicial review is
options: the power of parliament to dissolve the courts
the power of the courts to declare laws or executive acts unconstitutional
the appointment of judges by the legislature
questions.explanation:
Concept: Judicial review is the power of courts to declare laws or executive acts invalid if they conflict with the constitution.
Step 1: Recall the role of the courts.
Step 2: They review the constitutionality of laws and acts.
Step 3: Reject parliament dissolving courts, legislative appointment of judges and re-election.
Answer: the power of the courts to declare laws or executive acts unconstitutional.
Common mistake: It is not about re-electing judges.
Similar example: The Supreme Court in Marbury v Madison (1803) established judicial review in the USA.
Tip: Review = test for constitutionality.

questions.text: In Nigeria, the Council of State advises
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Council of State advises the President on matters such as prerogative of mercy, the National Population Commission and INEC. Its members include former presidents and heads of state, governors and the Chief Justice.
Step 1: Recall the role of the Council of State.
Step 2: It advises the President.
Step 3: Reject the Senate, Chief Justice and Inspector-General.
Answer: the President.
Common mistake: The Council does not make laws.
Similar example: The Council of State also advises on the maintenance of public order.
Tip: Council of State = Presidential advisers.
questions.topic: Institutions of Government in Post-Independence Nigeria

questions.text: A writ of habeas corpus is an order requiring
options: a bill to be read three times
that a detained person be brought before a court
questions.explanation:
Concept: Habeas corpus is a writ that orders the authorities to bring a detained person to court, so that the legality of the detention can be tested.
Step 1: Recall the meaning: 'you shall have the body'.
Step 2: It protects persons from unlawful detention.
Step 3: Reject bills, ministers' resignations and dissolution of government.
Answer: that a detained person be brought before a court.
Common mistake: It has nothing to do with legislative procedure.
Similar example: A court may use habeas corpus to free a person held without charge.
Tip: Habeas corpus = produce the person.

questions.text: The doctrine of 'ultra vires' refers to
options: acts done beyond legal power or authority
questions.explanation:
Concept: Ultra vires is Latin for 'beyond the powers'. An action done outside the legal authority of the person or body is ultra vires and invalid.
Step 1: Translate: 'ultra vires' means beyond the powers.
Step 2: It applies to acts done without legal authority.
Step 3: Reject acts within powers, acts approved by the legislature and sovereign acts.
Answer: acts done beyond legal power or authority.
Common mistake: Intra vires means 'within the powers'.
Similar example: A minister who makes a regulation that the Act does not allow acts ultra vires.
Tip: Ultra = beyond.

questions.text: The preamble to a constitution
options: states the aims and philosophy of the constitution
questions.explanation:
Concept: The preamble introduces a constitution, stating its aims and guiding principles. The Nigerian preamble begins with 'We the people'.
Step 1: Recall the function of a preamble.
Step 2: It states the aims and philosophy.
Step 3: Reject the list of arms, the amendment procedure and the schedules.
Answer: states the aims and philosophy of the constitution.
Common mistake: The amendment procedure is in the body of the constitution (section 9).
Similar example: The preamble to the 1999 Constitution speaks of one indivisible and indissoluble sovereign nation.
Tip: Preamble = Introduction.

questions.text: An alien is
options: a foreigner residing in a country who is not its citizen
questions.explanation:
Concept: An alien is a foreigner who lives in a country but is not its citizen. Aliens have fewer rights than citizens.
Step 1: Recall who an alien is.
Step 2: A foreign resident who is not a citizen.
Step 3: Reject citizens by birth, registration or naturalisation.
Answer: a foreigner residing in a country who is not its citizen.
Common mistake: A naturalised citizen is no longer an alien.
Similar example: A Ghanaian working in Lagos without Nigerian citizenship is an alien.
Tip: Alien = non-citizen.

questions.text: A civil servant is
options: an elected member of the legislature
a person employed in a government ministry or department
questions.explanation:
Concept: A civil servant is a permanent, non-political employee in a ministry or department who carries out government policy.
Step 1: Recall the meaning.
Step 2: He works in a ministry or department.
Step 3: Reject elected legislators, political appointees and private contractors.
Answer: a person employed in a government ministry or department.
Common mistake: A minister is a political appointee, not a civil servant.
Similar example: A permanent secretary is the senior civil servant of a ministry.
Tip: Civil servant = career government worker.

questions.text: The Code of Conduct Bureau was set up to
options: promote integrity of public officers, including receiving their asset declarations
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Code of Conduct Bureau promotes honest conduct by public officers. They declare their assets on assuming and leaving office.
Step 1: Recall the role of the CCB.
Step 2: It receives asset declarations and enforces the Code of Conduct.
Step 3: Reject conducting elections, recruiting civil servants and allocating revenue.
Answer: promote integrity of public officers, including receiving their asset declarations.
Common mistake: Elections are INEC's job.
Similar example: The Code of Conduct Tribunal tries breaches.
Tip: CCB = public officers' integrity.
questions.topic: Public Commissions Established by the 1979 and Subsequent Constitutions

questions.text: The Federal Civil Service Commission is responsible for
options: allocating revenue among tiers of government
appointment, promotion and discipline of federal civil servants
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Federal Civil Service Commission appoints, promotes and disciplines federal civil servants.
Step 1: Recall the role of the commission.
Step 2: It handles the career management of federal civil servants.
Step 3: Reject conducting elections, revenue allocation and prosecution.
Answer: appointment, promotion and discipline of federal civil servants.
Common mistake: Revenue allocation is the job of the RMAFC.
Similar example: A civil servant dismissed for misconduct may be disciplined by the commission.
Tip: FCSC = hire, promote, discipline.
questions.topic: Public Commissions Established by the 1979 and Subsequent Constitutions

questions.text: The Nigeria Police Force is headed by the
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Inspector-General of Police heads the Nigeria Police Force, appointed by the President on the advice of the Police Council.
Step 1: Recall the head of the police.
Step 2: It is the IGP.
Step 3: Reject the Chief of Defence Staff (armed forces), the Comptroller-General (customs) and the Attorney-General.
Answer: Inspector-General of Police.
Common mistake: The Chief of Defence Staff heads the armed forces.
Similar example: The Comptroller-General heads the Customs or Immigration service.
Tip: IGP = Police chief.
questions.topic: Institutions of Government in Post-Independence Nigeria

questions.text: Anonymity in the civil service implies that
options: civil servants are not credited or blamed in public for decisions of their ministers
civil servants may campaign for any party
civil servants take public credit for policy success
civil servants are elected by the public
questions.explanation:
Concept: Anonymity means that civil servants are not named or blamed in public for government policy. The minister takes the credit or blame.
Step 1: Recall the idea behind anonymity.
Step 2: Civil servants stay in the background.
Step 3: Reject campaigning for a party, taking public credit and election by the public.
Answer: civil servants are not credited or blamed in public for decisions of their ministers.
Common mistake: Civil servants are not allowed to campaign for parties.
Similar example: A minister defends a policy in the National Assembly, not the permanent secretary.
Tip: Anonymity = unnamed and unblamed.

questions.text: Under communism, the state is expected eventually to
options: wither away in a classless society
questions.explanation:
Concept: Marx predicted that under communism a classless society would emerge and the state would eventually wither away.
Step 1: Recall Marx's theory of the state.
Step 2: The state would disappear in a classless society.
Step 3: Reject expansion through private wealth, aristocratic rule and church control.
Answer: wither away in a classless society.
Common mistake: A stronger state is not the final aim in Marxist theory.
Similar example: Marx called the stage before communism the dictatorship of the proletariat.
Tip: Communism = classless, stateless.

questions.text: A welfare state is one that
options: provides social services such as health and education for its citizens
questions.explanation:
Concept: A welfare state provides social services such as health care, education and social security, so that citizens' basic needs are met.
Step 1: Recall what 'welfare' means.
Step 2: The state provides social services.
Step 3: Reject abolishing taxes, military control and banning unions.
Answer: provides social services such as health and education for its citizens.
Common mistake: A welfare state needs taxes to pay for services.
Similar example: The British National Health Service is a welfare programme.
Tip: Welfare = well-being.

questions.text: Nationalism is best described as
options: strong loyalty to one's nation and desire for its self-determination
ownership of industry by the state
questions.explanation:
Concept: Nationalism is a strong loyalty to one's nation and a desire for its freedom and self-determination. It drove independence movements in Africa.
Step 1: Recall the definition.
Step 2: It combines loyalty and the wish for self-rule.
Step 3: Reject foreign rule, a one-party state and state ownership.
Answer: strong loyalty to one's nation and desire for its self-determination.
Common mistake: Rule by foreign powers is colonialism, which nationalists opposed.
Similar example: Nigerian nationalists like Azikiwe and Awolowo worked for independence.
Tip: Nationalism = love of nation.

questions.text: In a single-member constituency system,
options: several representatives are elected per constituency
one representative is elected per constituency
questions.explanation:
Concept: In a single-member constituency, voters elect one representative for the constituency, usually the candidate with the most votes.
Step 1: Read the term: single member.
Step 2: Each constituency has one representative.
Step 3: Reject several representatives, a single party and unopposed elections.
Answer: one representative is elected per constituency.
Common mistake: Multi-member constituencies elect more than one representative.
Similar example: Nigeria's House of Representatives uses single-member constituencies.
Tip: Single-member = one winner per seat.

questions.text: A government formed by two or more political parties is called a
questions.explanation:
Concept: A coalition government is formed by two or more parties, usually when no party has a majority.
Step 1: Recall how governments form without a majority.
Step 2: Parties join to form a coalition.
Step 3: Reject caretaker, military and unitary governments.
Answer: coalition government.
Common mistake: A caretaker government is temporary and not formed by party partnership.
Similar example: Germany often has coalition governments.
Tip: Coalition = cooperation.

questions.text: A distinguishing feature of a political party is that it
options: seeks only to influence policy without contesting elections
aims to win and control political power
questions.explanation:
Concept: A party seeks power through elections and aims to win and control government. A pressure group only seeks influence.
Step 1: Recall the main aim of a party.
Step 2: It is to win and control political power.
Step 3: Reject influencing policy without contesting (pressure group), charity and agency.
Answer: aims to win and control political power.
Common mistake: Seeking influence without contesting is a pressure group feature.
Similar example: Parties field candidates in elections.
Tip: Party = power.

questions.text: Gerrymandering is
options: the manipulation of constituency boundaries to favour a party or candidate
questions.explanation:
Concept: Gerrymandering is drawing constituency boundaries unfairly to favour a party. It is named after Governor Elbridge Gerry of Massachusetts.
Step 1: Recall the definition.
Step 2: It is the manipulation of boundaries.
Step 3: Reject vote buying, vote counting and double voting.
Answer: the manipulation of constituency boundaries to favour a party or candidate.
Common mistake: Vote buying is bribery, not gerrymandering.
Similar example: A district with an odd shape that groups a party's supporters is a sign of gerrymandering.
Tip: Gerrymander = Gerry + salamander.

questions.text: Voter apathy refers to
options: lack of interest in voting or political participation
questions.explanation:
Concept: Voter apathy is lack of interest in elections and politics. It causes low turnout.
Step 1: Recall the meaning of apathy.
Step 2: It means indifference.
Step 3: Reject rigging, violence and multiple registration.
Answer: lack of interest in voting or political participation.
Common mistake: Rigging and violence are malpractices.
Similar example: Low turnout in an election may show voter apathy.
Tip: Apathy = indifference.

questions.text: The title of the ruler of the old Kanem-Bornu Empire was
questions.explanation:
Concept: The ruler of Kanem-Bornu was called the Mai. The Shehu later replaced the Mai in Bornu.
Step 1: Recall the title of the ruler.
Step 2: It was Mai.
Step 3: Reject Emir (Fulani), Alaafin (Oyo) and Oba (Benin and Yoruba).
Answer: Mai.
Common mistake: Alaafin is the Oyo title.
Similar example: Kanem-Bornu was one of the longest-lasting states in West Africa.
Tip: Kanem-Bornu = Mai.

questions.text: The traditional ruler of the Benin Kingdom is the
questions.explanation:
Concept: The ruler of the Benin Kingdom is the Oba, assisted by chiefs such as the Uzama and Eghaevbo n'Ore.
Step 1: Recall the title.
Step 2: It is Oba.
Step 3: Reject Alaafin (Oyo), Emir and Sultan (Hausa-Fulani).
Answer: Oba.
Common mistake: The Alaafin is the ruler of Oyo.
Similar example: The present Oba of Benin is a hereditary monarch.
Tip: Benin = Oba.

questions.text: The Royal Niger Company received its charter in
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Royal Niger Company, led by George Goldie, got a British royal charter in 1886 and controlled trade and administration in the Niger area.
Step 1: Recall the year.
Step 2: It was chartered in 1886.
Step 3: Reject 1861 (Lagos), 1900 and 1914.
Answer: 1886.
Common mistake: 1861 is the annexation of Lagos.
Similar example: The company's rights were taken over by the British in 1900.
Tip: RNC = 1886 charter.

questions.text: Lagos was annexed by the British in
questions.explanation:
Concept: Lagos was annexed by Britain in 1861, after Oba Dosunmu signed the Treaty of Cession under naval pressure.
Step 1: Recall the year of annexation.
Step 2: It was 1861.
Step 3: Reject 1851, 1886 and 1914.
Answer: 1861.
Common mistake: 1851 was the bombardment of Lagos.
Similar example: Lagos became a Crown Colony in 1862.
Tip: Lagos = 1861.

questions.text: Indirect rule was most successful in
questions.explanation:
Concept: Indirect rule succeeded in the North because centralised emirates already existed. The British used the emirs and the taxation system to rule.
Step 1: Recall where indirect rule worked.
Step 2: It worked best in the North.
Step 3: Reject the East, West and Niger Delta.
Answer: Northern Nigeria.
Common mistake: In the East it failed because of the lack of strong chiefs.
Similar example: Lugard used the emirate structure.
Tip: North = emirs = success.

questions.text: The Macpherson Constitution of 1951 was unique because it was
options: produced after wide consultations from the village to the national level
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Macpherson Constitution of 1951 was drafted after wide consultation, from village level to a General Conference at Ibadan.
Step 1: Recall the way it was made.
Step 2: It followed nationwide consultations.
Step 3: Reject military decree, a referendum and the Berlin Conference.
Answer: produced after wide consultations from the village to the national level.
Common mistake: It was not imposed.
Similar example: It started the ministerial system at the centre.
Tip: Macpherson = consultations.

questions.text: Under the Lyttelton Constitution of 1954, Lagos was made
options: the capital of the Western Region
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Lyttelton Constitution of 1954 made Lagos a federal territory, separate from the Western Region.
Step 1: Recall the status of Lagos.
Step 2: It became federal territory.
Step 3: Reject the capital of the West, part of the East and a trust territory.
Answer: a federal territory.
Common mistake: Lagos was never part of the Eastern Region, and it stayed the federal capital until 1991.
Similar example: Abuja replaced Lagos as federal capital in 1991.
Tip: Lyttelton = federal Lagos.

questions.text: The two political parties created by the Babangida regime in 1989 were the
options: National Party of Nigeria and Unity Party of Nigeria
Alliance for Democracy and All Peoples Party
Social Democratic Party and National Republican Convention
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Babangida regime created two parties in 1989: the Social Democratic Party (SDP) and the National Republican Convention (NRC).
Step 1: Recall the two parties.
Step 2: They were SDP and NRC.
Step 3: Reject NPN and UPN (Second Republic), NCNC and AG, and AD and APP.
Answer: Social Democratic Party and National Republican Convention.
Common mistake: NPN and UPN were Second Republic parties.
Similar example: SDP was a little left of centre and NRC a little right.
Tip: 1989 = SDP and NRC.
questions.topic: Political Parties and Party Politics in Post-Independence Nigeria

questions.text: The annulled presidential election of June 12, 1993 was contested by
questions.explanation:
Concept: The June 12, 1993 presidential election was contested by Moshood Abiola of the SDP and Bashir Tofa of the NRC. General Babangida annulled it.
Step 1: Recall the candidates.
Step 2: They were Abiola and Tofa.
Step 3: Reject the pairs from earlier republics.
Answer: Moshood Abiola and Bashir Tofa.
Common mistake: Awolowo and Shagari contested in 1979.
Similar example: The annulment led to political crisis and the interim government.
Tip: June 12 = Abiola v Tofa.

questions.text: The Organisation of African Unity was founded in
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Organisation of African Unity (OAU) was founded in Addis Ababa on 25 May 1963 by 32 independent African states.
Step 1: Recall the year.
Step 2: It was 1963.
Step 3: Reject 1960, 1975 and 1945.
Answer: 1963.
Common mistake: 1975 is the year of ECOWAS.
Similar example: The OAU became the African Union in 2002.
Tip: OAU = 1963.

questions.text: Nigeria became a member of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries in
questions.explanation:
Concept: Nigeria joined OPEC in 1971. OPEC was formed in 1960 in Baghdad.
Step 1: Recall the year of Nigeria's membership.
Step 2: It was 1971.
Step 3: Reject 1960, 1975 and 1980.
Answer: 1971.
Common mistake: 1960 is the year OPEC was founded.
Similar example: Nigeria is a leading African producer in OPEC.
Tip: OPEC = 1960; Nigeria joined 1971.

questions.text: Political participation refers to
options: activities through which citizens take part in choosing leaders and influencing policies
questions.explanation:
Concept: Political participation covers the ways citizens take part in politics: voting, joining parties, campaigning, contacting officials, protesting and standing for office.
Step 1: Recall what 'participation' means: taking part.
Step 2: Citizens take part in choosing leaders and influencing policy.
Step 3: Reject rigging (a malpractice), law enforcement (an executive duty) and paying tax only (a duty, not participation).
Answer: activities through which citizens take part in choosing leaders and influencing policies.
Common mistake: Election rigging is the opposite of healthy participation.
Similar example: A citizen who joins a party and votes is participating in politics.
Tip: Participation = taking part.

questions.text: A government is said to be accountable when
options: its officials must explain and justify their actions to the public or the legislature
questions.explanation:
Concept: Accountability means that those who hold public office must explain and justify their actions to the people or their representatives, and accept the consequences.
Step 1: Recall the idea of accountability: being answerable.
Step 2: Officials must explain and justify what they do.
Step 3: Reject ruling without consultation, being above the law and serving for life.
Answer: its officials must explain and justify their actions to the public or the legislature.
Common mistake: Being above the law is the opposite of accountability.
Similar example: A minister who answers questions in the legislature is accountable.
Tip: Accountable = answerable.

questions.text: Which of the following is a feature of a state but not necessarily of a nation?
questions.explanation:
Concept: A state must have sovereignty, territory, population and government. A nation is a cultural community. Sovereignty belongs to the state, not to the nation.
Step 1: Separate the cultural features (language, history, culture) from the legal feature (sovereignty).
Step 2: Only a state must have sovereignty.
Step 3: Reject common language, shared history and common culture, which describe a nation.
Answer: Sovereignty.
Common mistake: A nation can exist without sovereignty, for example the Kurds.
Similar example: Nigeria is a sovereign state that contains many nations.
Tip: Sovereignty = state.

questions.text: A major weakness of federalism is
options: duplication of functions and high cost of administration
questions.explanation:
Concept: Federalism has disadvantages: duplication of functions, high costs of running several governments and possible conflicts between levels of government.
Step 1: Ask which option is a weakness.
Step 2: Duplication and high administrative cost are weaknesses.
Step 3: Reject accommodation of diversity, local initiative and prevention of tyranny, which are strengths.
Answer: duplication of functions and high cost of administration.
Common mistake: Prevention of tyranny is an advantage of federalism.
Similar example: Having 36 state governments and a federal government is costly.
Tip: Federalism = costly but flexible.

questions.text: The doctrine that parliament can make or unmake any law is known as
questions.explanation:
Concept: Parliamentary sovereignty is the principle that parliament is the supreme law-making body in Britain and can make or unmake any law. No court can strike down an Act.
Step 1: Recall the principle in the question.
Step 2: It is parliamentary sovereignty.
Step 3: Reject judicial review (courts test laws), separation of powers and checks and balances.
Answer: parliamentary sovereignty.
Common mistake: Judicial review gives the courts power over laws, which is the opposite.
Similar example: In the UK, an Act of Parliament cannot be declared unconstitutional.
Tip: Britain = parliament is supreme.

questions.text: The Chief Justice of Nigeria is the head of the
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Chief Justice of Nigeria is the head of the judiciary and presides over the Supreme Court.
Step 1: Identify the arm headed by the Chief Justice.
Step 2: It is the judiciary.
Step 3: Reject the executive (the President), the legislature (Senate President) and the civil service (Head of Service).
Answer: judiciary.
Common mistake: The President heads the executive.
Similar example: The Chief Judge heads a state High Court.
Tip: CJN = judiciary.

questions.text: The House of Representatives of Nigeria has
questions.explanation:
Concept: The House of Representatives has 360 members, elected from single-member constituencies, while the Senate has 109.
Step 1: Recall the size of the House.
Step 2: It is 360.
Step 3: Reject 109 (Senate), 469 (total members of the National Assembly) and 36 (the states).
Answer: 360 members.
Common mistake: The total of both chambers is 109 + 360 = 469.
Similar example: If the Senate has 109 and the House has 360, the National Assembly has 469 members.
Tip: Reps = 360.

questions.text: Sittings of the Nigerian Senate are presided over by the
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Senate President presides over the Senate. The Speaker presides over the House of Representatives. Both are elected by their members.
Step 1: Recall who presides over the Senate.
Step 2: It is the Senate President.
Step 3: Reject the Speaker (House), Vice President (executive) and Chief Justice (judiciary).
Answer: Senate President.
Common mistake: The Vice President is not the Senate's presiding officer in Nigeria, unlike in the USA.
Similar example: The Senate President is the third-ranking officer after the President and Vice President.
Tip: Senate President = Senate.

questions.text: Meetings of the Federal Executive Council are presided over by the
options: Secretary to the Government of the Federation
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Federal Executive Council is the cabinet. It consists of the President, Vice President and ministers, and the President chairs it.
Step 1: Identify who chairs the Federal Executive Council.
Step 2: The President presides.
Step 3: Reject the Vice President, the Secretary to the Government and the Head of Service.
Answer: President.
Common mistake: The Vice President may chair in the President's absence but does not usually preside.
Similar example: The Secretary to the Government of the Federation is the secretary of the Council.
Tip: FEC = President in the chair.

questions.text: Impeachment of a state governor in Nigeria is initiated by the
questions.explanation:
Concept: Under section 188, a state governor can be impeached by the State House of Assembly for gross misconduct. A panel investigates and two-thirds of the members must vote for removal.
Step 1: Recall the body that begins impeachment of a governor.
Step 2: It is the State House of Assembly.
Step 3: Reject the Senate, Chief Judge and President.
Answer: State House of Assembly.
Common mistake: The Senate handles the impeachment of the President or Vice President, together with the House of Representatives, under section 143.
Similar example: A panel of seven persons is set up by the Chief Judge to investigate.
Tip: State governor = State Assembly.

questions.text: A characteristic of a written constitution is that it
options: is codified in one or more documents
questions.explanation:
Concept: A written constitution is set out in one or more documents. It states the structure and powers of government and the rights of citizens.
Step 1: Recall the meaning of a written constitution.
Step 2: It is codified in documents.
Step 3: Reject conventions only, no court interpretation and always flexible.
Answer: is codified in one or more documents.
Common mistake: A constitution based on conventions only is unwritten.
Similar example: Nigeria's 1999 Constitution is a written document.
Tip: Written = codified.

questions.text: A constitution that is difficult to amend is described as
questions.explanation:
Concept: A rigid constitution is difficult to change because it needs a special procedure, such as a high majority or approval by states.
Step 1: Recall the word for a constitution that is hard to amend.
Step 2: It is rigid.
Step 3: Reject flexible, unwritten and unitary.
Answer: rigid.
Common mistake: Flexible is the opposite.
Similar example: The American constitution is rigid.
Tip: Rigid = Hard to change.

questions.text: The right to a fair hearing in Nigeria is guaranteed mainly by
questions.explanation:
Concept: Section 36 of the 1999 Constitution guarantees the right to fair hearing, including a trial in public by an impartial court within a reasonable time.
Step 1: Recall the source of rights in Nigeria.
Step 2: The Constitution protects fair hearing.
Step 3: Reject decrees, the Police Act and the Land Use Act.
Answer: the Constitution.
Common mistake: Military decrees often removed rights.
Similar example: A person accused of a crime is presumed innocent until proved guilty.
Tip: Fair hearing = Section 36.

questions.text: The stage in the legislative process at which the general principles of a bill are debated is the
questions.explanation:
Concept: At second reading the general principles of a bill are debated. The bill can be rejected or sent to committee for detailed study.
Step 1: Recall the order of stages.
Step 2: General principles are debated at second reading.
Step 3: Reject first reading (introduction), third reading (final approval) and assent.
Answer: second reading.
Common mistake: First reading only introduces the title.
Similar example: Details are studied in committee after second reading.
Tip: Second reading = principles.

questions.text: A presidential veto in Nigeria can be overridden by
options: a simple majority of the Senate
a two-thirds majority of both chambers of the National Assembly
questions.explanation:
Concept: Under section 58 of the Constitution, the National Assembly can override a presidential veto by a two-thirds vote in both chambers.
Step 1: Recall how a veto is overridden.
Step 2: Two-thirds of both chambers can pass the bill.
Step 3: Reject a simple majority in the Senate, the Chief Justice and the Council of State.
Answer: a two-thirds majority of both chambers of the National Assembly.
Common mistake: A simple majority in one chamber is not enough.
Similar example: This is a legislative check on the executive.
Tip: Override = 2/3 of both.

questions.text: According to Max Weber, bureaucracy is characterised by
questions.explanation:
Concept: Max Weber described bureaucracy as organised by hierarchy, written rules, specialisation, impersonality and appointment by merit.
Step 1: Recall Weber's features of bureaucracy.
Step 2: Hierarchy and adherence to rules are central.
Step 3: Reject personal loyalty, the spoils system and absence of rules.
Answer: hierarchy and adherence to rules.
Common mistake: Personal loyalty is the opposite of impersonality.
Similar example: A civil servant who follows set procedures is acting bureaucratically.
Tip: Weber's bureaucracy = hierarchy + rules.

questions.text: The 'spoils system' is the practice of
options: ensuring neutrality in the civil service
rewarding party supporters with public jobs
questions.explanation:
Concept: The spoils system gives public jobs to loyal party supporters after an election. The American phrase is 'to the victor belong the spoils'.
Step 1: Recall the meaning of spoils.
Step 2: It is rewarding supporters with jobs.
Step 3: Reject merit recruitment, tenure and neutrality, which are features of a professional civil service.
Answer: rewarding party supporters with public jobs.
Common mistake: Merit-based recruitment is the opposite.
Similar example: Nigeria's civil service rejects this practice in principle.
Tip: Spoils = jobs for supporters.

questions.text: A system in which the state seeks to control all aspects of citizens' lives is
questions.explanation:
Concept: In totalitarianism, the state controls nearly all areas of life, including the economy, education and the media. Fascist Italy and Nazi Germany are examples.
Step 1: Recall the system with total state control.
Step 2: It is totalitarianism.
Step 3: Reject pluralism (many groups), federalism and liberalism.
Answer: totalitarianism.
Common mistake: Pluralism allows many independent groups.
Similar example: North Korea is often called a totalitarian state.
Tip: Total = totalitarian.

questions.text: Anarchists generally advocate
options: the abolition of the state and government
questions.explanation:
Concept: Anarchism rejects the state and all forms of compulsory government. Anarchists believe that society can run without rulers.
Step 1: Recall the aim of anarchism.
Step 2: It wants the abolition of government.
Step 3: Reject state ownership (socialism), monarchy and military rule.
Answer: the abolition of the state and government.
Common mistake: Anarchism is not the same as socialism.
Similar example: Mikhail Bakunin was an anarchist thinker.
Tip: An-archy = no ruler.

questions.text: An advantage of a multi-party system is that it
options: gives voters a wider choice and represents diverse interests
questions.explanation:
Concept: A multi-party system gives voters a wide choice and allows different interests to be represented. It does not guarantee stability.
Step 1: Recall the benefits of several parties.
Step 2: Voters have more choice.
Step 3: Reject guaranteed stability, elimination of the opposition and one-party dominance.
Answer: gives voters a wider choice and represents diverse interests.
Common mistake: Coalition governments can be unstable.
Similar example: Nigeria's Fourth Republic is a multi-party system.
Tip: Multi-party = more choice.

questions.text: The Academic Staff Union of Universities is an example of
questions.explanation:
Concept: Interest groups protect the interests of their members, for example workers, doctors and lecturers. ASUU is a union of university lecturers.
Step 1: Identify what ASUU does.
Step 2: It protects the interests of academic staff.
Step 3: Reject political party, government agency and coalition government.
Answer: an interest (protective) pressure group.
Common mistake: ASUU does not contest elections.
Similar example: The Nigerian Union of Teachers is also an interest group.
Tip: Union = interest group.

questions.text: The mass media is called the 'fourth estate' because it
options: acts as a watchdog over the three arms of government
questions.explanation:
Concept: The mass media are called the fourth estate because they watch over the three arms of government and inform the public.
Step 1: Recall the role of the press.
Step 2: It acts as a watchdog over government.
Step 3: Reject making, enforcing or conducting elections, which are not media functions.
Answer: acts as a watchdog over the three arms of government.
Common mistake: The media are not an official arm of government.
Similar example: An investigative report on corruption is a watchdog function.
Tip: Fourth estate = watchdog.

questions.text: Which of the following is an electoral malpractice?
questions.explanation:
Concept: Ballot box stuffing means putting extra, fake ballots into a ballot box. It is an electoral malpractice.
Step 1: Sort the options into proper practices and malpractices.
Step 2: Registration, campaigning and public counting are proper.
Step 3: Ballot stuffing is a fraud.
Answer: Ballot box stuffing.
Common mistake: Public counting protects the vote.
Similar example: Multiple voting and vote buying are other malpractices.
Tip: Stuffing = cheating.

questions.text: The electoral system in which a second round is held if no candidate gets the required majority in the first is the
questions.explanation:
Concept: In a run-off or two-round system, if no candidate wins the required majority in the first round, the top candidates go to a second round.
Step 1: Recall the system that uses two rounds.
Step 2: It is the run-off system.
Step 3: Reject simple plurality, proportional representation and the list system.
Answer: two-round (run-off) system.
Common mistake: Plurality needs only one round.
Similar example: France elects its president through two rounds.
Tip: Run-off = second round.

questions.text: An absolute majority means
options: more than half of the votes cast
questions.explanation:
Concept: An absolute majority means more than half (over 50%) of the votes cast. A plurality is the highest number of votes, even if below 50%.
Step 1: Recall the meaning of absolute.
Step 2: It means over half of the votes.
Step 3: Reject the highest number of votes (plurality), two-thirds and unanimity.
Answer: more than half of the votes cast.
Common mistake: The highest number of votes can be less than half.
Similar example: In a race with 100 votes, 51 votes is an absolute majority.
Tip: Absolute = over 50%.

questions.text: In the Sokoto Caliphate, emirs were appointed and confirmed by the
questions.explanation:
Concept: In the Sokoto Caliphate, the Sultan appointed and confirmed the emirs, who ruled the emirates under him.
Step 1: Recall who invested emirs.
Step 2: It was the Sultan.
Step 3: Reject the Alaafin (Oyo), the Governor-General (colonial) and age grades (Igbo).
Answer: Sultan.
Common mistake: The Governor-General was a colonial official.
Similar example: Later, under indirect rule, the British Resident confirmed emirs.
Tip: Sultan appoints emirs.

questions.text: A feature of the traditional Yoruba political system was
options: an Oba who ruled with a council of chiefs
questions.explanation:
Concept: Yoruba kingdoms had a hereditary Oba who ruled with a council of chiefs. The Alaafin of Oyo had the Oyo Mesi.
Step 1: Recall the Yoruba system.
Step 2: A king ruled with chiefs.
Step 3: Reject no king, age-grade-only rule and a caliph.
Answer: an Oba who ruled with a council of chiefs.
Common mistake: Age-grade rule is an Igbo feature.
Similar example: The Oba of Benin also ruled with chiefs.
Tip: Yoruba = Oba + chiefs.

questions.text: In traditional Igbo society, 'Ozo' was
options: a social and political rank acquired by wealthy and respected persons
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Ozo title was a high rank in Igbo society. It was taken by wealthy and respected men who performed ceremonies and paid fees.
Step 1: Recall what Ozo means.
Step 2: It is a title that shows status.
Step 3: Reject military rank, colonial title and tax collector.
Answer: a social and political rank acquired by wealthy and respected persons.
Common mistake: It was not a colonial invention.
Similar example: An Ozo title-holder had social and political influence.
Tip: Ozo = Igbo title.

questions.text: A major defect of indirect rule in Nigeria was that it
options: widened the differences between the North and the South
questions.explanation:
Concept: Indirect rule widened the gap between North and South because the British ruled the North through emirs and discouraged Christian missions and Western education there.
Step 1: Recall the weaknesses of indirect rule.
Step 2: It encouraged regional differences.
Step 3: Reject abolishing rulers, promoting unity and introducing universal suffrage.
Answer: widened the differences between the North and the South.
Common mistake: Indirect rule strengthened traditional rulers, so it did not abolish them.
Similar example: North and South developed differently in education and politics.
Tip: Indirect rule = North/South gap.

questions.text: The Nigerian Youth Movement was founded in
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Nigerian Youth Movement was formed in 1934 by young men such as H. O. Davies and Ernest Ikoli. It was the first truly nationalist organisation.
Step 1: Recall the year.
Step 2: It was 1934.
Step 3: Reject 1923 (NNDP), 1944 (NCNC) and 1951 (AG).
Answer: 1934.
Common mistake: 1923 was the NNDP.
Similar example: The NYM demanded self-rule and Nigerian unity.
Tip: NYM = 1934.

questions.text: The Northern People's Congress (NPC) was led by
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Northern People's Congress (NPC) began in 1949 as a cultural group and became a party. Its leader was Sir Ahmadu Bello, the Sardauna of Sokoto.
Step 1: Recall the leader of the NPC.
Step 2: It was Ahmadu Bello.
Step 3: Reject Awolowo (AG), Azikiwe (NCNC) and Aminu Kano (NEPU).
Answer: Sir Ahmadu Bello.
Common mistake: Balewa was deputy leader of the NPC.
Similar example: Bello was Premier of the Northern Region.
Tip: NPC = Bello.

questions.text: The first Prime Minister of independent Nigeria was
questions.explanation:
Concept: Abubakar Tafawa Balewa was the Prime Minister of Nigeria from 1957 to 1966. He was a member of the NPC.
Step 1: Recall the first Prime Minister.
Step 2: It was Balewa.
Step 3: Reject Bello (Premier of the North), Azikiwe (President) and Awolowo (Premier of the West).
Answer: Abubakar Tafawa Balewa.
Common mistake: Azikiwe was the first President, not Prime Minister.
Similar example: Balewa was killed in the January 1966 coup.
Tip: PM = Balewa.

questions.text: The body that debated the draft of the 1979 Constitution was the
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Constituent Assembly was set up in 1977 to debate the draft prepared by the Constitution Drafting Committee. Its work led to the 1979 Constitution.
Step 1: Recall the body that debated the draft.
Step 2: It was the Constituent Assembly.
Step 3: Reject the Supreme Military Council, Senate and Council of State.
Answer: Constituent Assembly.
Common mistake: The drafting was done by the committee, not the assembly.
Similar example: The Constitution Drafting Committee was led by Chief F. R. A. Williams.
Tip: CDC drafts, CA debates.

questions.text: The Mid-Western Region was carved out of the
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Mid-Western Region was created in 1963 from the Western Region, making four regions. It followed the 1962 political crisis in the Western Region.
Step 1: Recall which region was divided.
Step 2: It was the Western Region.
Step 3: Reject the Eastern and Northern Regions and Lagos.
Answer: Western Region in 1963.
Common mistake: The North and East were not divided in 1963.
Similar example: Benin was the capital of the Mid-West.
Tip: Mid-West = 1963 = from West.
questions.topic: The Structure and Workings of Nigerian Federalism

questions.text: The twelve states in Nigeria were created in 1967 by
questions.explanation:
Concept: In 1967 General Yakubu Gowon created twelve states by decree, dividing the four regions to weaken the secessionist threat.
Step 1: Recall who created the 12 states.
Step 2: It was Gowon.
Step 3: Reject Murtala (1976), Ironsi (no states) and Babangida (1987 and 1991).
Answer: Yakubu Gowon.
Common mistake: Murtala created seven new states in 1976, making 19.
Similar example: Six of the states were in the North and six in the South.
Tip: 12 states = Gowon.
questions.topic: The Structure and Workings of Nigerian Federalism

questions.text: The military coup of July 1975 brought to power
questions.explanation:
Concept: In July 1975 Brigadier Murtala Muhammed took power after a bloodless coup that removed General Gowon.
Step 1: Recall who took over in July 1975.
Step 2: It was Murtala Muhammed.
Step 3: Reject Obasanjo (his deputy and successor), Buhari (1983) and Ironsi (1966).
Answer: Murtala Muhammed.
Common mistake: Obasanjo took over after Murtala was killed in 1976.
Similar example: Murtala created seven states and began the move to Abuja.
Tip: 1975 = Murtala.

questions.text: The Second Republic in Nigeria ended in
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Second Republic began in October 1979 under Shagari and ended on 31 December 1983, when the military overthrew him.
Step 1: Recall the end date of the Second Republic.
Step 2: It was 1983.
Step 3: Reject 1979 (start), 1966 and 1993.
Answer: 1983.
Common mistake: 1979 is when the Second Republic began.
Similar example: The coup brought General Muhammadu Buhari to power.
Tip: Second Republic: 1979-1983.

questions.text: The head of the Interim National Government of 1993 was
questions.explanation:
Concept: Ernest Shonekan headed the Interim National Government from August to November 1993. General Sani Abacha forced him out.
Step 1: Recall the head of the interim government.
Step 2: It was Shonekan.
Step 3: Reject Abacha, Abubakar and Obasanjo.
Answer: Ernest Shonekan.
Common mistake: Abacha ousted the interim government.
Similar example: The interim government was set up after Babangida stepped aside.
Tip: ING = Shonekan.

questions.text: Nigeria's policy of non-alignment means that Nigeria
options: does not take sides in conflicts between major power blocs
questions.explanation:
Concept: Non-alignment means refusing to join the Cold War military blocs led by the USA and USSR. Nigeria followed it in its foreign policy.
Step 1: Recall the meaning of non-alignment.
Step 2: Nigeria does not take sides in great-power conflicts.
Step 3: Reject joining NATO or the Warsaw Pact and avoiding all foreign relations.
Answer: does not take sides in conflicts between major power blocs.
Common mistake: Non-alignment is not isolation.
Similar example: Nigeria is a member of the Non-Aligned Movement.
Tip: Non-aligned = no bloc.

questions.text: The African Union replaced the Organisation of African Unity in
questions.explanation:
Concept: The African Union (AU) replaced the Organisation of African Unity in 2002 and was launched in Durban, South Africa.
Step 1: Recall the year of the AU.
Step 2: It was 2002.
Step 3: Reject 1963 (OAU), 1975 and 1999.
Answer: 2002.
Common mistake: The Sirte Declaration of 1999 proposed the AU, but it was launched in 2002.
Similar example: The AU's headquarters is in Addis Ababa.
Tip: OAU 1963 → AU 2002.

questions.text: 'Who gets what, when and how' is a definition of politics by
questions.explanation:
Concept: Harold Lasswell, an American political scientist, defined politics as 'who gets what, when and how' in his 1936 book.
Step 1: Recall the author of the phrase.
Step 2: It is Harold Lasswell.
Step 3: Reject David Easton (authoritative allocation of values), Karl Marx and Max Weber.
Answer: Harold Lasswell.
Common mistake: Easton defined politics as the authoritative allocation of values.
Similar example: Lasswell's definition focuses on how resources are shared.
Tip: Lasswell = who gets what.

questions.text: The right of a citizen to vote and be voted for is a
questions.explanation:
Concept: Political rights are those that let citizens take part in government, for example voting, standing for election and joining political parties.
Step 1: Recall the types of rights.
Step 2: Voting and being voted for are political rights.
Step 3: Reject social, economic and cultural rights, which cover welfare, work and culture.
Answer: political right.
Common mistake: A right to work is an economic right.
Similar example: Freedom to join a political party is a political right.
Tip: Political right = vote and be voted for.

questions.text: The theory that the state originated as an instrument by which one class dominates another is the
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Marxist theory says that the state arose to protect the interests of the dominant economic class and to keep other classes down.
Step 1: Recall the theory that stresses class domination.
Step 2: It is the Marxist theory.
Step 3: Reject social contract (agreement), divine right (God) and force theory (conquest).
Answer: Marxist theory.
Common mistake: The force theory says the state arose from conquest, not class conflict.
Similar example: Marx expected the state to disappear in a classless society.
Tip: Marxist = class.

questions.text: The divine right theory holds that rulers derive their authority from
questions.explanation:
Concept: The divine right theory says that kings rule because God chose them. Subjects must obey, and the king answers only to God.
Step 1: Recall the source of authority.
Step 2: It is God.
Step 3: Reject the people (social contract), force and the constitution.
Answer: God.
Common mistake: Social contract theory puts authority in the people.
Similar example: James I of England defended the divine right of kings.
Tip: Divine right = from God.

questions.text: In an absolute monarchy, the monarch
options: shares power with an elected legislature
questions.explanation:
Concept: In an absolute monarchy, the monarch has unlimited power and is not bound by a constitution or legislature.
Step 1: Recall the meaning of 'absolute'.
Step 2: It means unlimited.
Step 3: Reject sharing power, bound by a constitution and ceremonial.
Answer: wields unlimited power.
Common mistake: A ceremonial monarch is a constitutional monarch.
Similar example: Louis XIV of France was an absolute monarch.
Tip: Absolute = no limits.

questions.text: The executive arm of government is responsible for
options: enforcement of laws and administration of the state
questions.explanation:
Concept: The executive carries out laws and runs the day-to-day affairs of the state, including policy, defence and administration.
Step 1: Recall the function of the executive.
Step 2: It enforces laws and administers.
Step 3: Reject making laws (legislature), interpreting laws (judiciary) and settling disputes (courts).
Answer: enforcement of laws and administration of the state.
Common mistake: Settling disputes between citizens is for the courts.
Similar example: The President and the ministers make up the executive.
Tip: Executive = execute.

questions.text: A bicameral legislature is advantageous because it
options: provides a second chamber to review legislation
questions.explanation:
Concept: A bicameral legislature has two chambers. The second chamber can review and improve the work of the first.
Step 1: Recall the advantage of two chambers.
Step 2: It provides a second review of bills.
Step 3: Reject faster lawmaking, cost reduction and executive dominance.
Answer: provides a second chamber to review legislation.
Common mistake: Two chambers usually slow down lawmaking.
Similar example: The Nigerian National Assembly is bicameral.
Tip: Bicameral = double check.

questions.text: In Nigeria, the power to make laws for the Federal Capital Territory is vested in the
questions.explanation:
Concept: The National Assembly makes laws for the Federal Capital Territory. State Houses of Assembly make laws for their states.
Step 1: Recall who legislates for the FCT.
Step 2: It is the National Assembly.
Step 3: Reject State Houses of Assembly, Supreme Court and Council of State.
Answer: National Assembly.
Common mistake: FCT is not a state and has no House of Assembly.
Similar example: The FCT has area councils instead of local governments.
Tip: FCT = National Assembly.

questions.text: The legislative bodies of Nigerian states are called
questions.explanation:
Concept: Each Nigerian state has a unicameral House of Assembly that makes laws for the state.
Step 1: Recall the name of a state legislature.
Step 2: It is the House of Assembly.
Step 3: Reject Senate and National Assembly (federal) and Council of Chiefs.
Answer: Houses of Assembly.
Common mistake: The Senate is a federal chamber.
Similar example: The number of members in a state House of Assembly is at least 24 and at most 40.
Tip: State = House of Assembly.

questions.text: A local government council in Nigeria is headed by a
questions.explanation:
Concept: A local government council is headed by a chairman, who is elected, with councillors as members of the legislative arm.
Step 1: Recall the head of a council.
Step 2: It is the chairman.
Step 3: Reject governor (state), emir (traditional) and commissioner (state ministry).
Answer: chairman.
Common mistake: Governors head states, not local governments.
Similar example: The chairman is the chief executive of the council.
Tip: LGA = Chairman.

questions.text: An advantage of a unitary system of government is that it
options: ensures uniform policies and quick decision-making
questions.explanation:
Concept: A unitary system has a single centre of authority, which makes it easy to apply uniform policy and decide quickly.
Step 1: Recall the strengths of a unitary system.
Step 2: It gives uniform policies and quick decisions.
Step 3: Reject diversity, constitutional division of power and local autonomy, which are federal features.
Answer: ensures uniform policies and quick decision-making.
Common mistake: Constitutional division of power is federal.
Similar example: France is a unitary state with centralised administration.
Tip: Unitary = uniform and quick.

questions.text: The 'residual list' in a federal system consists of
options: matters reserved to the federal government
matters not assigned to any level and left to the component units
questions.explanation:
Concept: The residual list consists of subjects not listed as federal or concurrent. In Nigeria these belong to the states.
Step 1: Recall what 'residual' means: what is left.
Step 2: These are matters left to the component units.
Step 3: Reject federal matters, local council functions and judicial powers.
Answer: matters not assigned to any level and left to the component units.
Common mistake: Federal matters are on the exclusive list.
Similar example: The USA also leaves residual powers to the states.
Tip: Residual = remainder.

questions.text: Disputes between a state and the Federal Government in Nigeria are resolved by the
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Supreme Court has original jurisdiction in disputes between the Federal Government and a state, or between states.
Step 1: Recall the court for federal disputes.
Step 2: It is the Supreme Court.
Step 3: Reject the Court of Appeal, Federal High Court and Customary Court.
Answer: Supreme Court.
Common mistake: The Court of Appeal hears appeals, not first-instance disputes of this kind.
Similar example: The Supreme Court is also the final court of appeal.
Tip: Federation disputes = Supreme Court.
questions.topic: Institutions of Government in Post-Independence Nigeria

questions.text: The supremacy of the constitution means that
options: the president is above the constitution
all laws and acts of government must conform to the constitution
it can be changed by decree at any time
questions.explanation:
Concept: Supremacy of the constitution means that the constitution is the highest law, and any inconsistent law is void. Section 1 of the 1999 Constitution says so.
Step 1: Recall the meaning of supremacy.
Step 2: All laws must conform.
Step 3: Reject the President above the constitution, ignoring it and changing by decree.
Answer: all laws and acts of government must conform to the constitution.
Common mistake: No person or body is above the constitution.
Similar example: A court can strike down a law that conflicts with it.
Tip: Supreme = highest law.

questions.text: Freedom of association includes the right to
options: form or belong to political parties and trade unions
questions.explanation:
Concept: Freedom of association lets people form or join groups such as unions and parties for lawful purposes. Section 40 protects it.
Step 1: Recall the right.
Step 2: It covers parties and unions.
Step 3: Reject private armies, disobeying laws and taking over government by force.
Answer: form or belong to political parties and trade unions.
Common mistake: Rights are used within the law.
Similar example: Workers can form a union under this right.
Tip: Association = join or form groups.

questions.text: A function of the civil service is to
options: advise ministers and implement government policies
questions.explanation:
Concept: Civil servants advise ministers on policy and put government policies into effect.
Step 1: Recall the role of the civil service.
Step 2: It advises and implements.
Step 3: Reject making laws, conducting elections and judging cases.
Answer: advise ministers and implement government policies.
Common mistake: Lawmaking belongs to the legislature.
Similar example: A permanent secretary advises the minister.
Tip: Civil service = advise + implement.

questions.text: The agency that investigates and prosecutes economic and financial crimes in Nigeria is the
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) investigates and prosecutes financial crimes such as fraud and money laundering.
Step 1: Recall the agency.
Step 2: It is the EFCC.
Step 3: Reject INEC (elections), NJC (judges) and CCB (asset declarations).
Answer: Economic and Financial Crimes Commission.
Common mistake: The CCB receives asset declarations but does not prosecute financial crimes.
Similar example: The ICPC also deals with corruption.
Tip: EFCC = Economic and Financial Crimes.
questions.topic: Public Commissions Established by the 1979 and Subsequent Constitutions

questions.text: A function of public opinion in a democracy is that it
options: influences government policies and checks abuse of power
questions.explanation:
Concept: Public opinion shapes government policy because leaders need public support. It also checks abuse of power.
Step 1: Recall the role of public opinion.
Step 2: It influences policies and checks abuses.
Step 3: Reject appointing judges, enforcing orders and making the constitution.
Answer: influences government policies and checks abuse of power.
Common mistake: Judges are appointed by the executive and the legislature, not by opinion.
Similar example: Mass protests can force a government to reverse a policy.
Tip: Opinion = influence + check.

questions.text: Opinion polls are usually conducted through
options: sampling a section of the population
questions.explanation:
Concept: Opinion polls ask a sample of the population about an issue. The sample must be representative.
Step 1: Recall how polls work.
Step 2: They sample a section of the population.
Step 3: Reject asking everyone, newspapers only and decree.
Answer: sampling a section of the population.
Common mistake: Asking the whole population is a census or referendum.
Similar example: A poll of 1,500 voters represents a country's views.
Tip: Poll = sample.

questions.text: The party that won the 1979 presidential election in Nigeria was the
questions.explanation:
Concept: The National Party of Nigeria (NPN) won the 1979 presidential election with Shehu Shagari as its candidate.
Step 1: Recall the winner in 1979.
Step 2: It was the NPN.
Step 3: Reject UPN, GNPP and PRP, which were rival parties.
Answer: National Party of Nigeria.
Common mistake: The UPN of Awolowo came second.
Similar example: NPN was the ruling party in the Second Republic.
Tip: 1979 = NPN.
questions.topic: Political Parties and Party Politics in Post-Independence Nigeria

questions.text: The Fourth Republic in Nigeria began in
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Fourth Republic began on 29 May 1999, when Olusegun Obasanjo took office after General Abdulsalami Abubakar's transition.
Step 1: Recall the start of the Fourth Republic.
Step 2: It started in 1999.
Step 3: Reject 1979 (Second Republic), 1993 and 2003.
Answer: 1999.
Common mistake: 1979 started the Second Republic.
Similar example: The Third Republic was the planned but aborted transition in 1993.
Tip: Fourth Republic = 1999.

questions.text: The first Executive President of Nigeria was
questions.explanation:
Concept: Shehu Shagari became Nigeria's first Executive President in October 1979 under the new constitution.
Step 1: Recall the first Executive President.
Step 2: It was Shagari.
Step 3: Reject Obasanjo (military head of state), Buhari and Azikiwe (ceremonial president).
Answer: Shehu Shagari.
Common mistake: Azikiwe was a ceremonial President from 1963 to 1966.
Similar example: Shagari was overthrown in December 1983.
Tip: Executive President = Shagari.

questions.text: The Zikist Movement, formed in 1946, was
options: a radical nationalist movement inspired by Nnamdi Azikiwe
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Zikist Movement was formed in 1946 by young radicals who admired Nnamdi Azikiwe. It demanded immediate self-government.
Step 1: Recall the Zikists.
Step 2: They were radical nationalists.
Step 3: Reject ethnic militia, colonial police and trade union.
Answer: a radical nationalist movement inspired by Nnamdi Azikiwe.
Common mistake: It was not a military group.
Similar example: Some of its leaders, such as Anthony Enahoro, were jailed for sedition.
Tip: Zikist = Zik's followers.

questions.text: The main objective of Pan-Africanism is
options: the unity and solidarity of African peoples
questions.explanation:
Concept: Pan-Africanism stresses unity, solidarity and freedom of African peoples everywhere. Kwame Nkrumah and others promoted it.
Step 1: Recall the goal.
Step 2: It is unity and solidarity.
Step 3: Reject colonial rule, isolation and capitalist expansion.
Answer: the unity and solidarity of African peoples.
Common mistake: Pan-Africanists opposed colonialism.
Similar example: The OAU grew out of Pan-African ideas.
Tip: Pan = all.

questions.text: Ghana's independence in 1957 influenced Nigerian nationalists because it was
options: the last colony to become independent
the first sub-Saharan African country to gain independence from colonial rule
questions.explanation:
Concept: Ghana gained independence in 1957 under Nkrumah as the first sub-Saharan colony to do so. This inspired Nigerian nationalists.
Step 1: Recall Ghana's significance.
Step 2: It was first in sub-Saharan Africa.
Step 3: Reject last colony, war and merger.
Answer: the first sub-Saharan African country to gain independence from colonial rule.
Common mistake: Ghana's independence was by negotiation, not by war.
Similar example: Nigeria followed in 1960.
Tip: Ghana = 1957 first.

questions.text: A feature of the pre-colonial Hausa-Fulani political system was
options: a hierarchy of title-holders and the application of Islamic law
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Hausa-Fulani system had emirs, title-holders and Islamic law. The Sultan stood at the head.
Step 1: Recall the features.
Step 2: It had a hierarchy and Islamic law.
Step 3: Reject rule by age grades, no taxation and no hierarchy.
Answer: a hierarchy of title-holders and the application of Islamic law.
Common mistake: The system had taxes such as kharaji and jangali.
Similar example: Judges called Alkalis applied Islamic law.
Tip: Hausa-Fulani = hierarchy + Sharia.

questions.text: The Ooni of Ife is regarded as
options: the spiritual head of the Yoruba
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Ooni of Ife is the spiritual head of the Yoruba, because Ile-Ife is regarded as the ancestral home and cradle of the Yoruba.
Step 1: Recall the role of the Ooni.
Step 2: He is the spiritual head.
Step 3: Reject Hausa head, Igbo head and colonial official.
Answer: the spiritual head of the Yoruba.
Common mistake: The Alaafin was the head of the Oyo empire, which was a political role.
Similar example: Oduduwa is said to be the ancestor of the Yoruba.
Tip: Ooni = spiritual.

questions.text: Which of the following Nigerian groups traditionally had a decentralised political system without a central king?
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Igbo traditionally had a decentralised system without a central king, based on villages, elders and age grades.
Step 1: Recall the group without a king.
Step 2: It was the Igbo.
Step 3: Reject the Hausa-Fulani, Oyo Yoruba and Benin, who had kings.
Answer: The Igbo.
Common mistake: Some Igbo areas like Nri and Onitsha had kings, but the common system was decentralised.
Similar example: Decisions were taken by assemblies.
Tip: Igbo = no central king.

questions.text: The 1960 Independence Constitution provided for a
questions.explanation:
Concept: At independence in 1960, Nigeria had a parliamentary system based on the British model, with a Prime Minister.
Step 1: Recall the system of 1960.
Step 2: It was parliamentary.
Step 3: Reject presidential, one-party and military.
Answer: parliamentary system of government.
Common mistake: Presidential government began in 1979.
Similar example: Balewa was Prime Minister under it.
Tip: 1960 = parliamentary.

questions.text: The first military Head of State of Nigeria was
questions.explanation:
Concept: General Johnson Aguiyi-Ironsi became Nigeria's first military Head of State in January 1966.
Step 1: Recall the first military Head of State.
Step 2: It was Ironsi.
Step 3: Reject Gowon (second), Murtala and Buhari.
Answer: General Aguiyi-Ironsi.
Common mistake: Gowon took over after Ironsi was killed in July 1966.
Similar example: Ironsi issued Decree No. 34, which turned Nigeria into a unitary state.
Tip: First military ruler = Ironsi.

questions.text: General Yakubu Gowon was overthrown in
questions.explanation:
Concept: General Gowon was overthrown in a bloodless coup on 29 July 1975 while attending an OAU summit in Kampala.
Step 1: Recall the date.
Step 2: It was 1975.
Step 3: Reject 1966, 1970 and 1979.
Answer: 1975.
Common mistake: Gowon took power in 1966.
Similar example: Murtala Muhammed replaced him.
Tip: Gowon out = 1975.

questions.text: General Olusegun Obasanjo handed over power to a civilian government in
questions.explanation:
Concept: General Obasanjo handed over power to the elected civilian President Shehu Shagari on 1 October 1979.
Step 1: Recall the year.
Step 2: It was 1979.
Step 3: Reject 1975, 1983 and 1976.
Answer: 1979.
Common mistake: He took power in 1976, after Murtala's death.
Similar example: He later became a civilian president in 1999.
Tip: Obasanjo handed over = 1979.

questions.text: The military regime that handed over power to a civilian government in May 1999 was led by
questions.explanation:
Concept: General Abdulsalami Abubakar became Head of State in June 1998 after Abacha died, and handed over to Obasanjo in May 1999.
Step 1: Recall the last military ruler before 1999.
Step 2: It was Abubakar.
Step 3: Reject Abacha, Babangida and Buhari.
Answer: General Abdulsalami Abubakar.
Common mistake: Abacha died in 1998 and did not hand over.
Similar example: The transition lasted about a year.
Tip: 1999 handover = Abubakar.

questions.text: The body that recommends the formula for sharing federally collected revenue is the
options: Revenue Mobilisation Allocation and Fiscal Commission
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Revenue Mobilisation Allocation and Fiscal Commission (RMAFC) recommends the formula for sharing the Federation Account among the three tiers of government.
Step 1: Recall the body.
Step 2: It is the RMAFC.
Step 3: Reject INEC, CCB and Public Complaints Commission.
Answer: Revenue Mobilisation Allocation and Fiscal Commission.
Common mistake: INEC runs elections, not revenue.
Similar example: The commission also monitors the accruals to the Federation Account.
Tip: RMAFC = revenue sharing.
questions.topic: Public Commissions Established by the 1979 and Subsequent Constitutions

questions.text: The Public Complaints Commission is Nigeria's
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Public Complaints Commission is an ombudsman. It investigates citizens' complaints against public officers and institutions.
Step 1: Recall the meaning of ombudsman.
Step 2: It handles complaints of maladministration.
Step 3: Reject electoral umpire, revenue body and police oversight.
Answer: ombudsman.
Common mistake: INEC is the electoral umpire.
Similar example: A citizen denied his pension can complain to it.
Tip: PCC = ombudsman.
questions.topic: Public Commissions Established by the 1979 and Subsequent Constitutions

questions.text: A major source of revenue for local governments in Nigeria is
options: statutory allocations from the Federation Account
questions.explanation:
Concept: Local governments get most of their revenue from the statutory allocation from the Federation Account, plus local taxes and fees.
Step 1: Recall the main source.
Step 2: It is the Federation Account.
Step 3: Reject oil exports, foreign loans and corporate tax.
Answer: statutory allocations from the Federation Account.
Common mistake: Corporate tax is collected by the federal government.
Similar example: Councils also collect market fees and tenement rates.
Tip: LG money = Federation Account.

questions.text: A function of local governments in Nigeria is
options: maintenance of markets, motor parks and refuse disposal
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Fourth Schedule of the 1999 Constitution lists functions of local governments, such as markets, motor parks, refuse disposal and primary education.
Step 1: Recall the functions.
Step 2: Markets and refuse disposal are local functions.
Step 3: Reject defence, currency and foreign affairs.
Answer: maintenance of markets, motor parks and refuse disposal.
Common mistake: Defence is federal.
Similar example: Councils also register births and deaths.
Tip: LG = markets and motor parks.

questions.text: Privatisation of public enterprises means
options: transfer of ownership of public enterprises to private individuals or firms
questions.explanation:
Concept: Privatisation is the transfer of ownership of state enterprises to private individuals or firms. It reduces government control.
Step 1: Recall the meaning.
Step 2: Ownership is transferred to private persons.
Step 3: Reject nationalisation (the opposite), new ministries and subsidies.
Answer: transfer of ownership of public enterprises to private individuals or firms.
Common mistake: Nationalisation is the reverse of privatisation.
Similar example: Selling a state-owned cement company to private investors is privatisation.
Tip: Privatise = make private.

questions.text: The headquarters of the African Union is located in
questions.explanation:
Concept: The headquarters of the African Union is in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.
Step 1: Recall the location.
Step 2: It is Addis Ababa.
Step 3: Reject Abuja, Lagos and Accra.
Answer: Addis Ababa.
Common mistake: ECOWAS is headquartered in Abuja.
Similar example: The AU Commission is located there.
Tip: AU = Addis Ababa.

questions.text: The Commonwealth of Nations is an association of
options: mostly former British colonies and territories
questions.explanation:
Concept: The Commonwealth of Nations is a voluntary association of mostly former British colonies.
Step 1: Recall the membership.
Step 2: Mostly former British colonies.
Step 3: Reject former French colonies, NATO and OPEC states.
Answer: mostly former British colonies and territories.
Common mistake: The French have the Francophonie.
Similar example: Nigeria joined at independence in 1960.
Tip: Commonwealth = ex-British.

topic_questions.text: A political system is more likely to remain stable when citizens accept its institutions as legitimate, even when they disagree with particular government policies. This situation best illustrates the importance of
topic_questions.explanation: Political legitimacy exists when citizens recognize and accept the authority of political institutions and leaders.

topic_questions.text: In a society where citizens acquire political attitudes mainly through family discussions, school activities, religious organizations and the mass media, the process involved is best described as
topic_questions.explanation: Political socialization is the process through which individuals acquire political values, attitudes and orientations.

topic_questions.text: A newly elected government introduces policies that are unpopular but constitutionally authorized. If citizens continue to obey the government because they recognize its lawful authority, the situation demonstrates
topic_questions.explanation: Political obligation refers to the willingness of citizens to recognize and comply with legitimate political authority.

topic_questions.text: When citizens deliberately avoid elections, political meetings and other lawful political activities because they believe their participation cannot influence government decisions, the behaviour is known as
topic_questions.explanation: Political apathy is a lack of interest or willingness to participate in political activities.

topic_questions.text: A political party organizes rallies, distributes campaign materials and encourages supporters to vote for its candidates. The primary political process being promoted is
topic_questions.explanation: Political mobilization involves encouraging and organizing citizens to participate in political activities.

topic_questions.text: In a community, young people who initially show little interest in public affairs become politically active after participating in student union elections and civic education programmes. This change is mainly an outcome of
topic_questions.explanation: Political socialization can develop political awareness and participation through institutions such as schools and associations.

topic_questions.text: A government that derives its authority from established constitutional procedures is fundamentally different from one that maintains power primarily through force because the former possesses greater
topic_questions.explanation: Constitutional authority generally provides legitimacy because power is exercised according to accepted legal procedures.

topic_questions.text: The tendency of individuals to develop political beliefs that resemble those of their parents, especially during childhood, demonstrates the influence of the
topic_questions.explanation: The family is usually one of the earliest and most influential agents of political socialization.

topic_questions.text: A citizen who writes petitions to government officials, attends peaceful political demonstrations and participates in public consultations is engaging primarily in
topic_questions.explanation: Political participation includes lawful activities through which citizens seek to influence public decisions.

topic_questions.text: Political participation is considered more meaningful in a democracy when citizens are able to
options: influence public affairs through lawful political activities
avoid all contact with political institutions
accept every government decision without criticism
allow only political elites to make public decisions
topic_questions.explanation: Meaningful participation allows citizens to influence political decisions through lawful means.

topic_questions.text: A political party selects some of its active members to contest legislative seats after assessing their leadership abilities and commitment to party policies. This activity is an example of
topic_questions.explanation: Political recruitment involves identifying and preparing individuals for political leadership or public office.

topic_questions.text: When citizens become increasingly detached from political institutions because they feel that government does not respond to their interests, the resulting condition is best described as
topic_questions.explanation: Political alienation occurs when individuals feel separated from or powerless within the political system.

topic_questions.text: Which situation most clearly demonstrates the role of the mass media as an agent of political socialization?
options: A newspaper explains the functions of government institutions to its readers
A court sentences a person for violating electoral laws
A parliament approves the national budget
A political party registers new candidates
topic_questions.explanation: The mass media contributes to political socialization by transmitting political information and values to citizens.

topic_questions.text: A government introduces civic education in secondary schools to teach students about constitutional rights, political institutions and responsible citizenship. The immediate political objective is to promote
topic_questions.explanation: Civic education helps individuals acquire political knowledge, values and attitudes, making it an important form of political socialization.

topic_questions.text: If voters support a candidate because they believe the candidate will protect their community's interests, their behaviour demonstrates that political participation may be influenced by
topic_questions.explanation: Political attitudes, interests and perceptions commonly influence how citizens participate in political activities.

topic_questions.text: A political culture in which citizens generally trust public institutions, obey lawful decisions and regard political participation as valuable is most likely to encourage
topic_questions.explanation: A supportive political culture can strengthen legitimacy, participation and stability in a democratic system.
